summary: A revision of the File Transfer Protocol from RFC 172. It adds two new file transfer requests, new error codes and editorial clarifications, then restates the protocol. FTP is a user-level protocol for moving files between ARPANET hosts. It was updated by several RFCs and replaced by RFC 354.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 265 describes an early FTP for moving files between ARPANET hosts. A user sends control commands to a server, which transfers file data over the data-transfer connection.

subtitle: A 1971 revision of the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol.

tldr.problem: ARPANET users needed a common way to transfer files among hosts with different file systems.
tldr.mechanism: FTP sends commands as control transactions over the Data Transfer Protocol and transfers file contents as data transactions. Requests include retrieve, create, store, append, rename, and delete.
tldr.outcome: RFC 265 revises RFC 172, was updated by RFCs 281, 294, and 310, and was obsoleted by RFC 354.

today: RFC 265 is obsoleted by RFC 354 and was updated by RFC 281, RFC 294, and RFC 310. It is an early stage in FTP's history.

sections.title: FTP Between ARPANET Hosts
sections.content:
FTP is a user-level protocol for file transfer between hosts on the ARPA Computer Network. Its objectives include sharing files, using remote storage, and shielding users from differences among hosts' file systems.

This RFC revises RFC 172. It adds two file transfer requests, changes opcode assignments, adds error codes for an incorrect or missing identifier and an existing file, and clarifies the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP lets a user request file operations on another host without needing to use that host's local file system directly. This revision adds requests and error codes to the earlier specification.

sections.title: Files, Names, and Data Types
sections.content:
A file is an ordered set of data identified by a pathname. FTP defines file-system commands but does not define a standard pathname convention; each user follows the server's local convention.

A set-data-type transaction can identify a data type and byte size. The default is an unspecified bit stream with a byte size of one, and a host must accept data even if it does not recognize the descriptor. The serving file system provides access control; FTP carries user name and password identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: A pathname identifies a file using the server's naming rules. The sender may describe the data, but the server controls access to its files.

sections.title: Requests and Data Transfer
sections.content:
The user initiates a full-duplex connection to the server's standard socket 3. Control transactions start with an opcode; standard requests include retrieve, create, store, append, append with create, delete, rename, and list.

Retrieve and list send data from server to user. Create, store, and append variants send data from user to server; the server acknowledges receipt. Rename from must be followed by rename to. The store request includes a four-byte allocate-size field before its pathname.
sections.plainLanguage: The user connects to socket 3 and sends a command that names a file operation. The direction of data and the required reply depend on the operation.

sections.title: Errors and Transaction Replies
sections.content:
An error transaction includes a code in its second information byte. Codes identify conditions such as access-control violation, an unsupported opcode, a failed file search, a missing identifier, or a file already present during a create request.

An error can end the current request sequence. The RFC says these errors concern file-transfer functions; data synchronization errors belong to the data-transfer protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: If a file request fails, the server can return a code describing the problem. Errors involving data synchronization are handled at the data-transfer level.
